dailyRead: The single most important fact this morning is a non-reaction. Overnight the US-Iran war produced its largest escalation to date: Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to transit Hormuz - two US ships, eight oil tankers and ten so-called non-compliant vessels - after US forces destroyed five Iranian tankers on Tuesday; Iran struck a US military base in Jordan, where the army shot down 18 missiles; and for the FIRST TIME the Guards extended their declared prohibited zone beyond the Strait itself into parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, with coordinates to follow. The IAEA board then referred Iran to the UN Security Council for nuclear non-compliance by 23 votes to 3 with 8 abstentions, Russia, China and Niger against. Brent breached 100 dollars for the first time since July, closing at 101.21 and trading 101.039 now, with WTI at 96.074 and up 15.49% on the month. And yet: GOLD IS DOWN 1.41% ON THE WEEK at 4,409.98. The Swiss franc is WEAKER on the week, USD/CHF at 0.80904 and +0.19%. The Canadian dollar did not move with crude at all - USD/CAD is 1.38060, unchanged today and UP 0.08% on the week. Three separate haven and terms-of-trade channels that should have fired did not. The conclusion this file draws, and it reframes every position on the board, is that the war's risk premium is now being paid entirely in ENERGY and no longer in currencies. The FX market has stopped trading the headline and gone back to trading central banks. That has two direct consequences today. First, XAU/USD is DOWNGRADED from LONG to RANGE: a gold position is a bet that geopolitical stress buys gold, and this week is the cleanest possible test of that proposition and gold failed it. Silver stays LONG at LOW-MED precisely because its industrial leg - it is +4.33% on the month against gold's +0.92% - is doing work gold's haven leg is not. Second, the yen keeps its +3 and its four HIGH-conviction expressions, because Japan is the one place where the policy repricing is live and accelerating: BoJ board member Masu said overnight at 01:39Z that the Bank expects to CONTINUE raising rates given accommodative financial conditions, and that further hikes are needed precisely to avoid being FORCED into rapid tightening later - naming Iran-driven fuel and chemical costs, distribution and food costs, yen pass-through and AI demand as persistent price pressures. That is the fourth hawkish confirmation in three sessions, on top of the upward-revised Q2 GDP, the Reuters Tankan at 21, machine tool orders +64.7%, average cash earnings +4.7% and Treasury Secretary Bessent's warning against betting against the currency. USD/JPY at 153.425 sits near a seven-month low with swaps carrying roughly 75bp of cumulative tightening by April 2027. On Europe: the euro's forward case genuinely hardened, and this file has now moved on it twice in three days, so the correction should be stated cleanly. Two days ago it said the ECB path was CLOSED on the September 3 Reuters poll, where 91% saw 2.50% as the year-end rate. Yesterday it softened that to 'economists closed the path, the ECB has not'. Today TradingEconomics states plainly that interest-rate futures are pricing in a THIRD hike by December, with previews putting the odds near 40-50%. Rate-market pricing outranks an economist poll, so the path is OPEN and the file was wrong to shut it. Against that, the gas tax got worse rather than better: EU gas is 79.1702 euros per MWh and +34.66% on the month with a 144.70% yearly gain, UK gas is 196.61 pence and +36.33% on the month, German storage is only 53% full against an EU aggregate of 65%, and Morgan Stanley has raised its winter TTF forecast to about 85 euros with risk skewed higher, writing that it is now too late for Qatari LNG to return before winter. EUR therefore holds +1 as a genuinely two-sided score with a hawkish forward tilt, and GER40 stays SHORT - an industrial economy entering winter with half-empty storage, a 36% monthly gas move and a central bank hiking into it. Sterling holds MINUS 1 with the worst gas exposure in G10 and a Bank frozen on September 17, though cable at 1.35552 is still up 0.22% on the week and GBP/USD stays LOW-MED for that reason - express sterling against the yen and the euro. The kiwi's rebound lasted exactly one session: NZD/USD is 0.58507 and now DOWN 0.50% on the week, so yesterday's 'the slide stopped' call was wrong within 24 hours and the RBNZ leg - a bank that hiked to 2.75% and then declined to validate an October follow-up - is doing the work, as it always was. AUD holds +2: consumer inflation expectations printed UNCHANGED at 4.9% this morning, elevated and sticky, with trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% and copper at 6.7676 and +2.90% on the week. CAD holds +1 but with an honest downgrade of its transmission: the oil leg is now at its cycle maximum and the currency is not monetising it, so the loonie is being traded on the -41,700 August jobs print and 2.0% wage growth instead, and every CAD cross stays a RANGE or a low-conviction expression. CHF holds +1 with the same note - it did not get the haven bid the escalation should have handed it, which caps rather than breaks the case. Today's binary is the ECB at 12:15Z; US PPI lands at 12:30Z and CPI tomorrow.

geopolitics: The war produced its largest escalation to date overnight and FX barely moved, which is the most important thing on this board today. The facts first. On Tuesday US forces destroyed FIVE Iranian oil tankers, directing the crews to abandon ship beforehand; Secretary of State Rubio said plainly that for every attempt Iran makes on a US naval vessel, 'they're going to lose tankers'. On Wednesday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and ten so-called non-compliant vessels attempting to transit the Strait, and UKMTO reported several merchant ships subject to disabling fire in both the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf. The Guards also struck a US military base in Jordan in retaliation; Jordan's army says it shot down 18 missiles. The genuinely new development, and the one that changes the geography of the risk, is that the Guards for the FIRST TIME extended their declared prohibited zone beyond the Strait itself into parts of the Gulf of Oman and the ARABIAN SEA, with spokesman Hossein Mohebi saying exact coordinates will follow and that any vessel entering without Iranian coordination will be subject to sanctions. Alongside the military escalation came a diplomatic one: the IAEA board of governors voted 23-3 with 8 abstentions to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over nuclear non-compliance, with Russia, China and Niger against. Iran's Guards named their terms for ending the war - no renewed threats, Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, an end to the Yemen blockade, release of USD 24 billion in frozen assets, and no interference in Iran's nuclear and missile programmes - while Netanyahu said Israel is 'very close' to bringing down the Iranian government. On timing, Trump asserted the conflict will end immediately after November's US midterm elections because Iran 'can't hold out any longer'; the Wall Street Journal quotes US officials saying his top advisers privately warn the war could drag on through the remaining two years of his term. That gap between the public and private timelines is the honest state of the de-escalation trade. One correction to this file's own framing: it has been carrying 'transits still run above nine million barrels a day against roughly twenty million pre-conflict' as a countervailing fact. AFP now reports that Iran has asserted control of the Strait since February with traffic VIRTUALLY PARALYSED, that Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees, and TradingEconomics describes the war as having CLOSED the Strait. The harder characterisation should be treated as the more current one, which makes the oil risk premium better justified rather than worse. Prices confirm: Brent breached 100 dollars for the first time since July, closing at 101.21 and trading 101.039; WTI is 96.074, up 5.25% on the week and 15.49% on the month; EU gas is 79.1702 euros per MWh and up 34.66% on the month and 144.70% on the year; UK gas is 196.61 pence and up 36.33% on the month. Now the part that matters for FX, and it is a negative result. Gold FELL 1.41% on the week to 4,409.98. The Swiss franc WEAKENED 0.19% on the week, USD/CHF at 0.80904. The Canadian dollar did not move at all as Brent broke 100 - USD/CAD is 1.38060 and UP 0.08% on the week. Three separate channels that should have transmitted this escalation into currencies did not. The conclusion this file draws is that the war's risk premium is now fully expressed in energy and no longer in FX, and that the currency market has gone back to trading central banks. Five consequences follow. First, XAU/USD is DOWNGRADED from LONG to RANGE - this week was the cleanest available test of the geopolitical-bid thesis and gold failed it; silver stays LONG only because its industrial leg, +4.33% on the month against gold's +0.92%, is doing independent work. Second, every CAD expression stays a RANGE or low-conviction until the loonie starts monetising its own terms of trade again; the market is trading the -41,700 August jobs print and 2.0% wage growth instead, and it is right to. Third, yesterday's argument that the franc is the cleanest European hedge against the gas shock should be held loosely - it is not visible in the price. Fourth, the gas channel remains the real FX transmission and it is a terms-of-trade TAX rather than a haven story: German storage is only 53% full against an EU aggregate of 65% and an Italian 83%, Morgan Stanley has raised its winter TTF forecast to about 85 euros with risk to the upside and says it is too late for Qatari LNG to return before winter, leaving Europe with its lowest storage in 15 years and almost no buffer to cold weather. That taxes EUR and GBP directly, lands on the ECB today, and keeps GER40 SHORT. Fifth, the entire tightening board still rests on this one input and the central banks say so explicitly - the RBA's August minutes list Middle East oil FIRST among the hike arguments, the BoC's September statement flags the continuation of the war as an upside inflation risk, the RBNZ attributes its 4.1% inflation largely to Middle East fuel prices, the BoE expects energy to lift CPI later this year, and BoJ board member Masu named Iran-conflict fuel and chemical costs among the persistent price pressures justifying further hikes. Five reaction functions from one input, which is also why the entire board would reprice together on a credible de-escalation headline. That single headline remains the largest correlated risk across every position in this file - and note that it is now a risk to the ENERGY leg far more than to the FX legs, since the FX market has already stopped paying for the war.
